description: Hi! I'm organizing OrbitCare AI for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Please contact me through the NASA Space Apps team page or Discord to discuss the project, share ideas, and coordinate our work.
summary: OrbitCare AI is an explainable astronaut health-monitoring prototype built on real NASA Open Science Data Repository data (OSD-575). It combines four blood-biomarker panels (metabolic, cardiovascular and two immune panels) from four crew members across seven mission phases, from before launch to 194 days after return. A dashboard shows trends against laboratory reference ranges, and a crew-alert engine compares each astronaut with their own pre-flight baseline, flagging deviations with plain-language reasons. Astronauts can also enter their own values by typing or voice. Rule-based checks decide what is flagged, and an LLM explains the results and answers questions. As missions get longer, crews will need monitoring that works with limited medical support. We chose transparent rules over a black-box model because the dataset is small, and we state its limits openly.
details:
What it does: OrbitCare AI has four parts. The Dashboard explores four NASA OSD-575 biomarker panels across seven mission phases (L-92, L-44, L-3, R+1, R+45, R+82, R+194), with reference ranges, a data-quality report and an AI explanation of the biggest changes. Crew Alerts compares each of the four crew members with their own pre-flight average using z-scores and percent change, and labels deviations Alert or Watch with a plain-language reason and a recovery check. My Health lets an astronaut enter blood values and symptoms by typing or voice; entries are saved and compared with NASA lab reference ranges and their own history. The AI assistant answers questions about the latest check-in, with read-aloud.

How it works: A Python script cleans the NASA files and reports missing values without inventing data. A Flask API serves the data and runs the rule-based alert engine. A React dashboard with Recharts visualizes it. An LLM (Google Gemini or Anthropic Claude via API) writes the explanations from the rule results. It never decides what is flagged. Emergency words trigger a fixed safety message, and if the AI is unavailable the app falls back to rule-based text.

Why rule-based: the dataset has only four crew members, so a machine-learning model would not be reliable. Every flag can be explained, which matters in a health setting. The app is a research prototype and not a medical device.

Impact: the same approach could support autonomous health monitoring on future long-duration missions and remote care on Earth.

Tools: Python, Flask, pandas, NumPy, React (Vite), Recharts, Gemini / Claude API, browser Web Speech API. Code was written with AI assistance (ChatGPT, Claude) and reviewed by our team.
projectRefs: Google Gemini API (LLM used inside the app)
Web Speech API (voice input and read-aloud)
